newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro shares above lows, dollar revives.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro shares above lows, dollar revives.

text.p: European stock markets slid lower in early business on Monday, taking their cue from Wall Street's second biggest points loss in history on Friday, but cut back their losses by the end of the morning.

Investors looked to Wall Street's reopening for pointers to what to do next amid uncertainty over whether the drop marked an end to a relentless rise in U.S. and European share prices or just a short-term correction.

"We see this as another periodic bout of profit-taking nervousness...There is some froth there to be taken out but nothing fundamental has changed," said Tony Robinson, head of equities at fund manager Lombard Odier.
U.S. stocks traded in London were generally above their lows.

"We're pretty much lower across the board but the initial panic selling was absorbed," one London dealer in U.S. shares said, while adding: "It's anyone's guess as to what (Wall Street) will eventually do."

A somewhat less negative outlook for stocks helped the dollar revive. It had earlier suffered from concern over the possibility of higher German interest rates in a week that holds key meetings of monetary policy makers in both the United States and Germany.

Gold, meanwhile, added a couple of dollars on bullion market hopes that stock market woes could send some funds its way but dealers said investors still seemed to lack trust in precious metals as safe havens.
A weak dollar and worries about U.S. profits wiped 247.37 points, or more than three percent, off the Dow Jones Industrial Average to 7,694.66 on Friday.

With that loss, the barometer of U.S. blue-chip stock prices had fallen 6.8 percent from its all-time closing high of 8,259.31 on August 6. But it was still more than 3,000 points or nearly 66 percent above its level two years ago.

Wall Street's fall spurred heavy selling on Monday on Asian markets, many of which are also being undermined by currency turmoil in the region. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average in Tokyo fell 1.47 percent.

Continental European markets, several closed on Friday for a holiday, were then generally hit more than London, Europe's largest stock market, which had already responded to the early stages of Friday's Dow plunge.

But London still had a tough start, with the FTSE 100 index opening with a loss of nearly 1.5 percent and extending this before reviving to a deficit of around half a percent by midsession as futures and bonds rallied.

The FTSE had tumbled 125.5 points or 2.5 percent on Friday, its largest loss in percentage terms in five years -- but compared with a much larger plunge of 250.7 points, or 12.22 percent, in the "crash" of October 20, 1987.

In Frankfurt floor trade the DAX index showed an early fall of about four percent but it had closed on Friday before Wall Street's retreat and halved its loss by late morning. The IBIS index for electronic trade was barely lower at midsession.

"We have to remember that the DAX has been a real performer this year and it was time for some sort of a correction," said one Frankfurt dealer, noting that the DAX had gained 55 percent since January while the Dow, no slouch, had added about 30 percent.
Paris, one of a number of markets closed on Friday for Assumption Day, was particularly hard hit with the CAC-40 down some 3.3 percent at one stage before staging a revival to halve its loss.
Overall, many market analysts now expect more selective investment strategies to come into favour after a long more general rally driven by the weight of money available.
The dollar recovered after being hit by jitters about higher German interest rates before the Bundesbank holds its first meeting on Thursday after the summer break.
"Fears of knock-on effect today from Friday's sell-off seem to have been overdone," said Sanjit Maitra, head of economics and strategy at WestLB in London.
"The market's focus is on German rates and a degree of nervousness will persist ahead of the repo tender and the council meeting."

Economists doubt whether the German central bank would move towards higher rates at Tuesday's repo tender or tighten credit after Thursday's council meeting since remarks showing German officials' concern about the mark's decline and inflation had already made an impact.
Markets are also awaiting news from the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee, which meets to consider interest rates on Tuesday but is not generally expected by economists to raise U.S. rates just yet.

The dollar/yen rate pushed higher again but stayed below 118 yen. It had been capped by remarks from U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang who expressed concern about Japanese trade data. Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus jumped almost 70 percent in July.
CURRENCIES AT 1130 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.8185 marks and 117.85 yen, compared with 1.8227 and 117.76 in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1130 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index was down 23.7 points or 0.49 percent at 4,842.1.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index for floor trade was 80.27 points or 1.93 percent lower at 4,072.59. The IBIS index for electronic trade was down just 3.52 points or 0.09 percent at 4,074.07.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index was 45.36 points or 1.55 percent lower at 2,876.48.
The Madrid stock market was down around 1.7 percent, Milan 1.9 percent, Stockholm 0.6 percent and Zurich 1.6 percent. The Amsterdam bourse was up 1.6 percent.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was quoted around $326.25 an ounce, compared with a morning fix of $326.05 and Friday's London close of $324.35. Silver gained nine cents to $4.54.
